string.text: A standard 20-gauge shotshell loaded with 6 mm buckshot. At close range it has tremendous killing and stopping power. Intended for use in smoothbore firearms only.

The 5.7x28 mm SS190 is a pistol cartridge created in 1986 to replace the 9x19 mm Parabellum. Compared to the 9x19 mm it offers a flatter trajectory, reduced recoil, greater effective range, improved armor penetration, and a lower tendency to ricochet. This cartridge occupies a niche between pistol and intermediate (rifle) cartridges. The 5.7x28 mm is used in the FN P90 personal defense weapon and the FN Five-seveN pistol.
The 5.7x28 SS195 JHP is a hollow-point cartridge with less penetrating power than the SS190, but greater stopping power and lethality.

.50 Action Express (also .50 AE, 12.7x33, 12.7x32.6 mm) is a cartridge developed in 1988 for the Israeli Desert Eagle pistol. One of the most powerful semi-rimmed pistol cartridges in the world. It features a flat-nosed bullet, which accounts for the cartridge's enormous stopping power.
Magnum (from Latin magnus - great, large) refers to a cartridge of higher power compared to a standard cartridge of the same caliber, as well as to firearms chambered for such a cartridge.
A Soviet 7.62 mm pistol cartridge. A simple full-metal-jacket bullet with a lead core.
A Soviet 7.62 mm pistol cartridge. Features a steel core bullet with improved armor penetration.
A Soviet 7.62 mm assault rifle cartridge (index 57-N-231). A simple jacketed bullet with a steel core.
A Soviet armor-piercing 7.62 mm assault rifle cartridge (index 7N23). Features a bullet with a heat-treated tool-steel core for improved armor penetration.
A NATO standard rifle cartridge. Caliber 7.62 mm. A simple jacketed bullet with a lead core.
A NATO standard armor-piercing rifle cartridge. Caliber 7.62 mm. Features a steel core bullet with improved armor penetration.
The standard military 7.62x54 mm PS sniper cartridge (index 7N1). The bullet has a blunt steel core. A cost-effective sniper cartridge modification for sniper rifles.

The AK104/AK105 are modifications of the AK-103 and AK74M respectively, with a barrel shortened by 101 mm. This intermediate barrel length (between the AK74M and AKS-74U) allowed the weapon's overall size to be reduced while keeping the gas port in the same position relative to the breech as in the AK74M, rather than moving it rearward as in the AKS-74U. This improved parts commonality across the entire "hundred series" family.

The M16 (official designation: Rifle, Caliber 5.56 mm, M16) is an American automatic rifle chambered in 5.56 mm, developed from the AR-15 and adopted in the 1960s. The M16 and its variants remain the primary weapon of US infantry to this day. It is one of the most widely produced small arms in the world, with over 8 million units manufactured.

The M16A1 is an improved variant of the M16. Key differences include: addition of a bolt forward assist, an improved bolt buffer (which lowered the cyclic rate to 750-850 rounds per minute and eliminated bolt bounce and misfires), a more reliable closed-prong flash hider, chrome-lined bolt (to prevent corrosion), a tighter rifling twist from 1:14 to 1:12 inches (which improved bullet stability but increased dispersion at ranges beyond 400 m), and a bayonet lug. A 30-round magazine and a suppressor designed for standard (rather than subsonic) cartridges were also created specifically for the new rifle. It served in the US Army from 1967 to 1985.

A Croatian submachine gun produced during the early period of the Yugoslav civil war. Used by self-defense units, partisan-insurgent formations, and sabotage-terrorist groups, as well as some Croatian Army units, though it was never officially adopted. The submachine gun proved popular among criminals, as the weapon was produced under wartime conditions, was never test-fired for police ballistic records, and (apart from individual display examples) was not even marked with serial numbers.

The 9 mm Stechkin Automatic Pistol is an automatic pistol developed in the late 1940s and early 1950s by designer I. Ya. Stechkin and adopted by the Soviet Armed Forces in 1951, simultaneously with the Makarov pistol. The APS is designed to arm officers engaged directly in combat, as well as soldiers and sergeants of certain special units.

The 9 mm Makarov Pistol Modernized (PMM, GRAU index 56-A-125M) is a Russian pistol developed in the early 1990s under the "Grach" R&D program. It participated in the competition for a new army pistol under the designation "Grach-3."
The 8x57 IS cartridge was the primary German Army cartridge during both World War I and World War II.

The most widely used cartridge in the German Army was the heavy pointed s.S (schweres Spitzgeschoss) bullet weighing 12.8 grams. Intended for firing from heavy and light machine guns, rifles, and carbines in service with the Wehrmacht.
Originally developed as a specialized sniper cartridge for long-range shooting, it is today also widely used by hunters and sport shooters.

The 12.7x55 mm STs-130 is a Russian rifle cartridge with a subsonic bullet velocity, developed at TsKIB SOO for silent and flameless engagement of protected targets and personnel in heavy body armor at ranges up to 600 meters.

The 12.7x99 mm cartridge (also known as .50 BMG and 12.7x99 mm NATO) is a large-caliber cartridge used by NATO armies. It was developed in the 1920s as a cartridge for the Browning M1921 heavy machine gun. After World War II the cartridge was standardized within NATO and is manufactured by member nations to common specifications.

A special sniper cartridge with subsonic bullet velocity, allowing its use in suppressed weapons during special operations. Thanks to its caliber it delivers high stopping power, and its heavy special-design bullet penetrates most body armor at ranges up to 200 meters.
An enhanced-penetration cartridge featuring an armor-piercing core of hardened tool steel. Designed to engage personnel sheltering behind light armor at ranges up to 500 m.

The 40 mm VOG-25P or "Podkidysh" (Bouncing Betty, 7P24) is a fragmentation grenade for grenade launchers whose key feature is a nose fuze that causes the grenade to bounce off the ground and detonate in the air, increasing its lethal effect.
